abstract.title: Abstract
abstract.p: Perovskite nanocrystals with CsPbX3 (X = Cl, Br, or I) structure have attracted great attention for developing optoelectronic applications in the past few years. However, their low stability and the limited scalability of current synthesis methods pose major challenges for future applications. Here, a template‐assisted strategy is reported for synthesizing CsPbCl3 nanocrystals within mesoporous silica nanoreactors. Powder state CsPbCl3 complex fabricated via this method demonstrated an exceptional solvent stability and allows for yttrium doping to further enhance optical performance. Halide tuning (Cl⁻ to Br⁻) and synthesis of lead‐free perovskites such as Cs4Bi2MnCl12 enable broad spectral emission, supporting full‐spectrum white LED fabrication. This low‐cost, scalable, and reproducible method offers strong potential for advancing perovskite‐based optoelectronic technologies.

Crystals under Control! Cesium lead halide perovskite nanocrystals (PNCs) are synthesized inside mesoporous silica nanoreactors, yielding highly stable and color‐tunable emitters. Yttrium doping enhances photoluminescence intensity of PNCs, while halide tuning adjusts emission colors. Combining these nanocrystals with Cs₄MnBi₂Cl₁₂ PNCs leads to a white‐light‐emitting LED with full‐spectrum tunability.

sec.title: Introduction
Materials
sec.p: All reagents were used as received without further purification, including cesium chloride (CsCl, from BioShop), lead chloride (PbCl2, from Sigma–Aldrich), yttrium(III) chloride (YCl3, from Sigma–Aldrich), dimethylformamide (DMF, from Fisher Scientific), dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO, from Fisher Scientific), Hydrochloric Acid (HCl, from Fisher Scientific), tetraethoxysilane (TEOS from Sigma–Aldrich), ethanol (from Fisher Scientific), diethanolamine (DEA, from Sigma–Aldrich), cetyltrimethylammonium (CTAB, from Sigma–Aldrich), acetone (from Fisher Scientific), Bismuth(III) oxide (Bi2O3, from Sigma–Aldrich), cesium carbonate (Cs₂CO₃, from Sigma–Aldrich), octadecene (ODE, from Sigma–Aldrich), oleic acid (OA, from Sigma–Aldrich), oleylamine (OLA from Sigma–Aldrich).

Fabrication of Mesoporous Silica Nanoparticle‐CsPbCl3 Nanocrystals matrix: Figure
1 illustrates the overall synthesis method. Briefly, 50 mg of pre‐synthesized mesoporous silica nanoparticles (MSNs) were mixed with 100 ul of solution containing a molar ratio of 1:1 of CsCl stock solution and PbCl₂ stock solution (lead chloride solvent system was composed of DMF/DMSO/HCl in a 7:2:1 volume ratio and cesium precursor solvent was composed of deionized water). The mixture was transferred into a long glass tube, sealed with parafilm, and a small hole was introduced at the top to allow vapor release. The tube was then placed in a vacuum oven (model: AT09‐316L‐UL; Across International) at 65 °C for 4 h to facilitate precursor infiltration. The resulting CsPbCl₃–MSN composite was subsequently transferred to crucible and calcined at 600 °C for 15 min (with a 1 h ramp time) to complete crystallization. Yttrium‐doped CsPbCl₃ was synthesized by introducing YCl₃ into the precursor mixture during the mixing stage. To produce CsPbX₃ (X = Cl, Br), CsCl and PbCl₂ were replaced with CsBr and PbBr₂ (lead salt was dissolved in a solvent system composed of DMF and DMSO in an 8:2 volume ratio).

sec.p: Fabrication of Mesoporous Silica Nanoparticle ‐Cs₄Bi₂MnCl₁₂ Nanocrystals matrix: Similar to MSN‐ lead halide PNCs synthesis, 50 mg of pre‐synthesized mesoporous silica nanoparticles (MSNs) were mixed with 100 ul of solution containing a molar ratio of 4:1:1 of CsCl stock solution, Bi2O3 stock solution and MnCl2 stock solution (Bi2O3 stock were prepared in a HCl solvent system). The mixture was transferred into a long glass tube, sealed with parafilm, and a small hole was introduced at the top to allow vapor release. The tube was then placed in a vacuum oven at 120 °C for 2 h to facilitate precursor infiltration and crystallization.

Cesium precursor solution: Cesium precursor solution was prepared by mixing Cs₂CO₃ (0.407 g), oleic acid (OA, 1 mL), and octadecene (ODE, 10 mL) in a 50 mL three‐necked flask. The mixture was heated to 120 °C under vacuum for degassing, followed by nitrogen purging. The solution was then maintained at 50 °C under nitrogen for later use.

Synthesis of CsPbCl₃ Nanocrystals: Lead precursor solution was prepared by dissolving PbCl₂ (0.37 mmol) in ODE (10 mL) in a 50 mL three‐necked round‐bottom flask. The mixture was degassed under vacuum while gradually heating to 90 °C for 30 min to remove residual air and moisture. The temperature was then increased to 120 °C, and the flask was purged with nitrogen three times before being maintained under a nitrogen atmosphere for 1 h. Subsequently, OA (1 mL) and oleylamine (OLA, 1 mL) were injected into the lead precursor solution at 120 °C to facilitate the complete dissolution of PbCl₂. The temperature was then raised to 170 °C, and 0.8 mL of the preheated cesium precursor solution was swiftly injected. Nanocrystal formation occurred rapidly upon injection. After 5 s, the reaction mixture was quenched by immersion in an ice‐water bath to rapidly cool the solution to room temperature and suppress further nanocrystal growth.

Fabrication of single chip white light photoluminescence driven LED: Yttrium‐doped CsPbCl₃–MSN, CsPbClBr₂–MSN, CsPbCl₁.₅Br₁.₅–MSN, CsPbCl₂Br–MSN, CsPbBr₃–MSN, and Cs₄Bi₂MnCl₁₂–MSN powders were blended with a UV‐transparent silicone gel. The mixture was solidified on a cap and mounted onto a GaN‐based UV LED chip with a peak emission at 370 nm. The optical performance of the resulting LED devices was characterized using a FluoroMax Plus spectrofluorometer (Horiba).

Characterizations: X‐ray diffraction (XRD) patterns were acquired on a Rigaku MiniFlex600 system with a Cu radiation. Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) images were taken from using Hitachi HT7700 with acceleration voltage of 80kV. SEM images and EDS mapping were taken from using Hitachi SU7000 with acceleration voltage of 15kV. The specific surface areas were calculated by the Brunauer–Emmett– Teller (BET) method. The total pore volume was obtained from the t‐plot method (N2, micromeritics, ASAP2460, USA). Pore size distribution was calculated from the adsorption branch of N2 adsorption/desorption isotherm and BET method. The PL spectra were prepared by using a FluoroMax Plus spectrophotometer with a Xe lamp excitation source from Horiba.

sec.title: Result and Discussion
sec.p:
To visually assess the water stability of CsPbCl₃–MSN, we compared its PL behavior with colloidal CsPbCl₃ PNCs synthesized via a previously reported hot‐injection method using OA and OLA as surface ligands. CsPbCl₃–MSN retained stable PL intensity for up to 14 days in aqueous dispersion (Figure
2a). In contrast, the 10nm‐colloidal CsPbCl₃ PNCs exhibited a rapid decline, losing ≈75% of their emission intensity within 10 min of water exposure and over 99% within 2 days (Figure 2b) (Figure S1, Supporting Information). To further evaluate the chemical stability of CsPbCl₃–MSN, the nanocomposites were dispersed in ethanol at room temperature for 14 days, with PL spectra recorded every 2 days. ≈85% of the initial emission intensity was retained after 14 days (Figure 2c). Additionally, a 50% DMF–H₂O mixed solvent was used to further challenge the stability, CsPbCl₃–MSN maintained more than 80% of its PL intensity after 14 days of dispersion (Figure 2d). In comparison, colloidal CsPbCl₃ PNCs no longer exhibit any emission immediately upon dispersion in either ethanol or 50% DMF–H₂O solution.

E) SEM image of template‐assisted yttrium‐doped CsPbCl₃ nanocrystals and EDS elemental maps.

a) Emission of CsPbX3(X = Cl,Br) and Cs₄Bi₂MnCl₁₂ PNCs synthesized by nanoreactor (excitation of 365 nm). b) Illustration of white color PL‐driven LED device. c) Image of PL‐driven LED setup turned on in darkroom. d) Luminance white LED under LED excitation. e) CIE1931 diagram of five recorded point from LED.

sec.p: To demonstrate the feasibility of fabricating color‐tunable LEDs, five samples were prepared with varying mixing ratios MSN‐PNCs matrices. The emission colors from each sample were characterized using a spectrofluorometer and plotted on the CIE diagram (Figure 4d,e). Emission of different MSN‐PNCs were also indicated in the diagram as they can be seen as the emission color boundary of such device. By blending the powders with silicone gel and assembling them using the described method, tunable emission colors were achieved under 370 nm LED excitation. These results confirm that MSN‐PNCs matrices are suitable for single‐chip, UV‐excited, color‐tunable LED fabrication. Due to the high stability of synthesized PNCs and the simple fabrication procedure of this method, commercializing such optoelectrical device based on PNCs can be achievable.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: In summary, we developed a facile and robust method for fabricating lead halide PNCs with excellent environmental stability, maintaining strong photoluminescence in various solvent conditions over extended periods. This approach enables the synthesis of doped CsPbCl₃ and lead‐free halide PNCs, making them suitable for color‐tunable white light LED applications. Owing to the reproducibility of the synthesis and the stability of the resulting nanocrystals, this method offers strong potential for commercialization of halide PNC‐based optoelectronic devices.
